text: Selling directly to a local trader, collector, or village buyer is often practical for a Preah Vihear smallholder because the buyer may come to the farm and take responsibility for transport and onward marketing — useful where farms are scattered, roads are difficult in the wet season, volumes are small, and the farmer lacks a truck or storage. Traders may buy rice, cassava, maize, cashew, vegetables, or livestock and aggregate from several farmers before reselling. A lower farm-gate price is not automatically exploitation — the trader is paying for transport, labor, aggregation, handling, losses, and market risk. The relevant calculation is net return after transport, loading, grading, storage, and spoilage, plus the value of receiving payment quickly. During the wet season (roughly May–October), muddy roads make transporting small quantities inconvenient, making farm-gate collection more attractive; during the dry season (roughly November–April), transport may be easier but farmers may face pressure to sell quickly for cash. Compare offers from more than one buyer when practical, clarify the unit/quality grade being used, and record price and payment received rather than assuming the highest advertised market price is the highest net price actually available. For livestock, a sick animal should never be transported to a trader — restrict movement and seek animal-health guidance instead. No specific local price, buyer, or crop variety is assumed for a Preah Vihear farmer without current verification.
